passage: I'm Jomon, and honestly, I didn't see it at first. Rafiq and I have shared a flat since first year. Last spring his school friend Asif went through a terrible breakup, and Rafiq became his everything: calls at two in the morning, skipped classes to sit with him, message after message all day. Then I noticed Rafiq had stopped cooking, stopped playing football, and once fell asleep in the shower. When I asked, he snapped, "If I don't answer and something happens, it's on me." Then he cried, because he also felt guilty for being tired of it. We sat down that night and made a plan. He'd tell Asif, kindly, that he loved him and couldn't be his only person. Asif's brother and the college counsellor would be brought in. Rafiq would keep his phone on silent after midnight unless it was an emergency. It felt harsh to him. It was actually what let him keep helping.

qa.q: What did Rafiq stop doing?
qa.a: Cooking and playing football.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq cry when Jomon asked?
qa.a: He felt guilty for being tired of helping, and afraid that if he didn't answer, anything bad would be his fault.

qa.q: Which part of the plan was hardest for Rafiq, and why was it still a wise choice?
qa.a: Keeping his phone on silent after midnight except in emergencies felt harsh, but it protected his sleep so he could keep helping.

qa.q: What is it like for Rafiq to set these limits?
qa.a: It feels harsh and guilty to him at first, but it gives him rest and shares the load with Asif's brother and the counsellor, so he isn't drained.

grounding: It shows Jomon noticing a young man becoming a friend's only support, drained and guilty, and helping him set kind limits and bring in others.

passage: I'm Omkar. I sit next to Jyoti at the design studio, so I saw most of it, though I can only guess what she felt. From June, she spent every lunch break in the stairwell on the phone, speaking softly: "I know, I know, I'm here." Her friend was going through something bad; that much she told me. By August she was eating biscuits for lunch and her eyes looked puffy most mornings. Once, when her phone buzzed during a client meeting, she went pale and apologised to everyone twice. In September something shifted. I overheard her say, "I care about you, and I can't be the only one. Can I call your mum with you tonight?" After that she took her full lunch break with us. Last Friday she even laughed at the terrible canteen dal. I don't know everything that happened, but she looks like she's breathing again.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti spend every lunch break from June?
qa.a: In the stairwell on the phone.

qa.q: What might Jyoti's pale face during the client meeting suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she may have been anxious that her friend needed her, and embarrassed about the interruption.

qa.q: What choice did Jyoti make in September?
qa.a: She told her friend she cared but couldn't be the only support, and offered to call the friend's mum together.

qa.q: How has the change affected Jyoti, as Omkar sees it?
qa.a: Omkar sees her taking full lunch breaks and laughing again, looking as if she can breathe after months of strain.

grounding: It shows Omkar, who sits beside her at work, watching a young woman drained by being a friend's only support, and seeing her recover once she sets a kind limit and involves others.

passage:
First week: Gautam, twenty, was the one Gurpreet called every night after her breakup. He listened till two in the morning, every night. She said, "You're the only one who gets it."
Third week: Gautam fell asleep in his statistics exam. He snapped at his roommate, then felt terrible. Worse, he felt a flash of resentment when Gurpreet's name lit up his phone, and then guilt for feeling it.
Fifth week: Gautam said to her, gently, "I care about you. I can talk till eleven, not later, or I'm no use to anyone. And I think your sister and the college counsellor should be in this too." Gurpreet was hurt for a day. Then she called her sister. Gautam slept eight hours for the first time in a month.

qa.q: What happened to Gautam in his statistics exam?
qa.a: He fell asleep in it.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel in the third week?
qa.a: He felt drained and resentful when Gurpreet called, then guilty for feeling that way.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that let him keep helping?
qa.a: He set a kind limit on call times, suggested her sister and the college counsellor also help, and started looking after his own sleep.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet react to Gautam's limit?
qa.a: She felt hurt for a day, but then reached out to her sister, widening her support.

grounding: Shows a friend drained and guilty as someone's only support, who sets kind limits, involves others and looks after his own health to keep helping.

passage: "Pema, you look so tired. Is it your friend again? Let me tell you about when I was twenty. My cousin Zara was struggling after her father died, and I became her everything. She called me at night, at college, at my aunt's wedding. I never said no. I stopped sleeping properly. I failed a paper. And I started to dread her calls, then hated myself for it. One night my mother found me crying and said, 'Afreen, you can't pour from an empty pot. Tell Zara's brother. Tell her teacher. And tell Zara what time you can talk.' I did. Zara was hurt at first. But with more people around her, she got stronger, and so did I. You're allowed to have limits, Pema."

qa.q: What did Afreen's mother say about pouring?
qa.a: 'You can't pour from an empty pot.'

qa.q: How did young Afreen feel about Zara's calls?
qa.a: Afreen felt exhausted and started to dread the calls, then felt guilty and self-hating for it.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped both cousins?
qa.a: Afreen's mother advised involving Zara's brother and teacher and set clear times, so Zara had more support and Afreen could rest.

qa.q: How might Zara have felt when Afreen set limits?
qa.a: Zara was hurt at first, but she grew stronger with more people supporting her.

grounding: An elder recalls being a cousin's only support, feeling drained and guilty, and learning to set kind limits and involve others to keep helping.

passage: It was the night before Gautam's final engineering exam, and his phone buzzed again. Joseph, his hostel friend, had been leaning on him for weeks since failing a semester. Every night Gautam listened, skipped revision and felt more exhausted. Tonight he felt a spike of irritation, then a wave of guilt. He took a breath and called back. "Joseph, I'm here, and I care. But I have an exam at nine. Can we talk for ten minutes now, and properly tomorrow after two?" He also said, "I think your brother should know how you're doing, and the counsellor too. You deserve more than just me." Joseph was quiet, then said, "Okay. I'll call my brother." Gautam studied till eleven and slept.

qa.q: What time was Gautam's exam?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when his phone buzzed again?
qa.a: He felt irritated and then guilty, worn out from weeks of being Joseph's main support.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that balanced care and his own health?
qa.a: He set a short, kind time limit, promised a proper talk later and encouraged Joseph to involve his brother and the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt hearing "You deserve more than just me"?
qa.a: Joseph may have felt a little hurt but also cared for, and agreed to call his brother.

grounding: Shows a friend drained and guilty from being the only support, who sets a kind limit, involves others and protects his own health despite exam pressure.

passage:
Zubin had shared a flat in Bandra with Payal for a year, and lately he'd started worrying about her.
Every night around one, her phone buzzed. It was always Rhea, her college friend, crying about her breakup and exam stress. Payal would sit on the balcony talking until three. She'd started missing her morning lectures. At breakfast she looked grey.
One morning Zubin found her asleep on the sofa, phone on her chest. When she woke, she said, "I'm so tired. But if I don't pick up, I feel like a terrible friend."
Zubin made her tea. "You can care about Rhea and still sleep. Who else does she have?"
"Her sister. The college counsellor, maybe."
"What if you told Rhea you'll talk before eleven, and help her reach them too?"
Payal was quiet. Then she typed the message, and switched her phone to silent at midnight.

qa.q: What time did Payal's phone usually buzz?
qa.a: Around one every night.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he watched Payal over those weeks?
qa.a: He felt worried and protective, seeing her exhausted and missing lectures.

qa.q: What did Zubin suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Setting a kind limit on call times and involving Rhea's sister and the college counsellor, so Payal can keep helping without burning out.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about the late-night calls?
qa.a: She feels drained and guilty, afraid that not answering would make her a terrible friend.

grounding: Zubin notices his flatmate becoming a friend's only support and feeling drained and guilty, and helps her set kind limits and involve others.
